articleOfWeek.title: Maternal and Fetal Outcomes in Pregnant Women with Burn Injuries: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articleOfWeek.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articleOfWeek.abstract: Burn injuries during pregnancy are associated with significant maternal and fetal morbidity and mortality; however, available evidence is fragmented and largely based on small observational studies. To estimate pooled maternal and fetal mortality among pregnant women with burn injuries and explore the impact of burn severity. A systematic review and meta-analysis of proportions was conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and LILACS were searched from inception to March 2026. Observational studies and case series reporting maternal and/or fetal outcomes were included. Risk of bias was assessed using Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and Joanna Briggs Institute tools, and certainty of evidence using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation. Random-effects models with Freeman-Tukey double arcsine transformation were applied. Results: Twenty-two studies including 1162 pregnant women were analyzed. Most studies were case series (n = 15), followed by cohort studies (n = 5) one cross-sectional study, and one case report. Maternal mortality ranged from 0% to 70%. The pooled maternal mortality proportion was 0.43 (95% CI, 0.36-0.50), with substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 72.9%). Fetal mortality ranged from 31.3% to 90.5%, with a pooled estimate of 0.57 (95% CI, 0.49-0.65; I2 = 78.6%). Burn severity, particularly TBSA burned ≥50%, was consistently associated with worse outcomes. Funnel plots suggested possible publication bias. The overall certainty of evidence was low. Burn injuries during pregnancy are associated with high maternal and fetal mortality, strongly influenced by burn severity. Despite consistent findings, the low certainty of evidence highlights the need for high-quality prospective studies.

articles.title: Classification Systems and Clinical Outcomes of Axillary Burn Contracture: A Systematic Review and Meta Analysis.
articles.journal: Journal of burn care & research : official publication of the American Burn Association
articles.abstract: Axillary burn contracture is a common and debilitating complication of burn injuries, impairing mobility and quality of life. Multiple classification systems and reconstructive techniques exist, but optimal management remains unclear due to limited systematic data comparing outcomes across techniques and classifications. A systematic review was performed. PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science were searched for full-text studies reporting surgical treatment of axillary contractures. Data extraction and quality assessment were performed independently by 2 reviewers. Outcomes were synthesized qualitatively, and recurrence rates were meta-analyzed using a random-effects model. Planned subgroup analyses by contracture type were not feasible due to inconsistent reporting. Of 1196 articles screened, 62 met inclusion criteria, encompassing 1602 patients. Most studies were observational. Formal classification systems were inconsistently applied; Kurtzman and Stern classification was the most common one (16.1%). Commonly reported surgical techniques included trapeze flap plasties (n = 277), skin grafting (n = 239), skin grafting with local flaps (n = 85), and Z-plasties (n = 85). Meta-analysis of 78 studies (855 reconstructions) demonstrated a pooled recurrence rate of 13.0% (95% CI, 10.7-15.8), with no heterogeneity (I2 = 0%). Meta-regression suggested higher recurrence rates with longer follow-up. Functional outcomes improved across studies, with flap-based reconstructions demonstrating greater gains in abduction (≈82°) than skin grafting (≈52°). In conclusion, flap-based techniques appear to provide lower recurrence and superior postoperative range of motion (ROM) compared to skin grafting. However, inconsistent classification, predominance of observational studies, and variable outcome reporting limit direct comparisons. Standardized classification, quantitative ROM metrics, and minimum follow up durations are needed to guide evidence-based surgical selection.

articles.title: 2026 International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation Consensus on Science With Treatment Recommendations: Summary from the Basic Life Support; Advanced Life Support; Pediatric Life Support; Neonatal Life Support; Education, Implementation, and Teams; and First Aid Task Forces.
articles.abstract: This is the annual summary of the International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation Consensus on Science With Treatment Recommendations; a comprehensive review was completed in 2025. This latest summary addresses the most recent published resuscitation evidence reviewed by International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation task forces, including Basic Life Support; Advanced Life Support; Pediatric Life Support; Neonatal Life Support; Education, Implementation, and Teams; and First Aid. Members from these 6 task forces assessed the certainty of the evidence using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation criteria, and their statements include consensus treatment recommendations. Highlights from task force discussions and insights into how decisions regarding treatment recommendations were made are provided in the Justification and Evidence-to-Decision Framework Highlights sections. The task forces also listed priority knowledge gaps for further research.

articles.title: Giving or Taking? Ethical Guidance for Hospital Administrators Involved in Organ Procurement.
articles.abstract: Organ procurement from unrepresented decedents is legal in the United States, and some states even designate "the hospital administrator" as having the right to authorize donation. However, there is little guidance for an administrator to consult in their effort to make a socially responsible decision. In this case study, we review the arguments in favor of deferring, deciding against, or deciding in favor of authorization. We contend that that there are three reasons involving uncertainty, inequity, and the risk of mistrust that should give an administrator pause in endorsing organ procurement. We ultimately recommend that organ recovery should not be authorized unless there is (1) strong evidence that a diligent search for surrogates has been undertaken, establishing a reasonable amount of certainty that none are forthcoming, and (2) some evidence suggesting that the decedent would favor organ donation.

articles.title: "Bold and necessary experiments:" The redelegation of authority and responsibility to nurses at the origins of cardiac intensive care.
articles.abstract: Coronary Care Units (CCUs) were at the forefront of the development of intensive care in the 1960s and 1970s. The development of CCUs, and intensive care more broadly, was enabled by the interplay of expanding medical technology and the evolving role of nurses vis-à-vis physicians. This paper examines the history the CCU at New York Hospital, the teaching hospital of Cornell University School of Medicine and School of Nursing, with a particular focus on role of nurses in the unit's success. Drawing from historical archives of New York Hospital and the Cornell University School of Nursing, this paper argues that that nurses were co-creators, alongside physicians, of the NYH CCU, and demonstrates how nurses drew from the NYH CCU experience to expand critical care services at the local and national level, including by advocating for the creation of the NYH medical intensive care unit (MICU), leading a CCU nurse training program to expand regional CCU capability, and contributing expertise to a federally-sponsored national conference on CCUs. A close reading of this history offers lessons and insights as intensive care medicine moves into an uncertain future, chief among them that work of caring for critically ill patients requires the thoughtful integration of new technologies with hands on care.

Efficiency of Rescue Paramedic Hoist versus Underslung Antenna in Helicopter-Based Avalanche Searches: A Randomized Trial.
articles.abstract: Survival for avalanche victims is time-dependent, and survival is often reliant on ground companion rescue. Due to the time-critical nature of burial, remote locations, and high frequency of concomitant severe trauma, helicopters are often dispatched to these incidents. While helicopter-based transceiver searches are standard, the most efficient deployment strategy, either using an underslung antenna or hoisting a rescue paramedic (RP) with a handheld transceiver, remains unknown. This study compared the operational efficiency of these two methods in the Norwegian Search-and-Rescue (SAR) Helicopter Service. A dual randomized, experimental field trial was conducted with the on-duty SAR helicopter and crew at the Ørland Main Airforce Base (Trøndelag, Norway). A simulated avalanche area of 80 × 150 meters was used, and six avalanche transceivers were buried at approximately 0.5m depth across the area. Only one transceiver was active at each run, and the locations were randomized to prevent crew memorization. The sequence of which procedure to use was also randomized. Four operational timestamps were recorded: First Signal, Optimal Signal, RP on Ground, and Transceiver Found. Over three days, a total of 25 trial runs were performed, 13 with Antenna Search and 12 with RP Hoist Search. The RP Hoist Search was significantly faster in both time to Optimal Signal, with a difference between the groups of 29 seconds (95% CI, 9 - 50), and time for RP on Ground, with a difference between the groups of 124 seconds (95% CI, 98 - 151). For the total time to Transceiver Found, the difference between the groups was 143 seconds (95% CI, 113 - 172; P <0.001). Furthermore, the RP Hoist Search resulted in significantly faster fine search on the ground. This randomized, experimental field trial comparing two currently used standard search procedures in the Norwegian SAR service showed that the RP Hoist Search was significantly more efficient than the Antenna Search for localizing buried avalanche victims, reducing total localization time by more than two minutes. Given that survival probability is reduced after 10-15 minutes of burial, this time saving may be clinically significant. The findings support that RP Hoist Search is an effective localization strategy for SAR helicopter services with comparable hoist systems.

articles.title: Learning at the bedside is not the same as reaching it.
Characterization of Urgent ICU Consultations in the Evaluation of Processes of Care and the Outcomes of Children in Hospital (EPOCH) Randomized Clinical Trial.
authors: Evaluation of Processes of Care and the Outcomes of Children in Hospital (EPOCH) Investigators
articles.abstract: Urgent ICU consultation is intended to elicit advice and consider ICU transfer. Our objective was to describe the nature and outcomes of ICU consultations across a global cohort. This is a secondary analysis of patients with one or more ICU consultations. A care episode was defined as consecutive urgent ICU consultations until an ICU admission or at least 2 weeks without an urgent ICU consultation. We describe consultation outcomes for the last care episode. Late escalations were defined by a Children's Resuscitation Intensity Scale score greater than 2. Twenty-one centers participating in the Evaluation of Processes of Care and the Outcomes of Children in Hospital (EPOCH) cluster-randomized trial. There were 4288 urgent ICU consultations in 3625 care episodes for 3000 patients with a median (interquartile range) age of 25 months (5-99 mo). In the parent EPOCH trial, hospitals were randomized to Bedside Pediatric Early Warning System or usual care; no intervention was assigned in this secondary analysis. The outcomes of the 3000 last care episodes were in-consultation death in three (0.1%) and urgent ICU admission in 1477 (49.2%). Among 3000 first, 400 second, and 68 third consultations, the proportions of ICU admission were 42%, 44%, and 47%. The proportions of ICU admissions that were late escalation were similar across groups: 18% for first and second urgent ICU consultations, and 25% for third urgent ICU consultations. among patients having a second urgent ICU consultation, patients who had received resuscitation interventions in their first urgent ICU consultation (and remained on the ward) had more frequent resuscitation events (23.2% vs. 3.4%, p < 0.01) and had a similar frequency of late escalation (31.8% vs. 15.6%, p = 0.07) and ICU admission (51.1% vs. 43.1%, p = 0.40) compared with patients without resuscitation in their first urgent ICU consultation. Urgent consultation to the ICU is common during pediatric hospitalization. Repeated ICU consultation was associated with a similar frequency of late escalation. Resuscitation measures were provided in one of 12 ICU consultations where patients were not admitted to ICU and were a risk factor for late escalation in subsequent consultations.

articles.title: Low Physical Activity and Reported Barriers Among Survivors of Critical Illness: A Mixed-Method Study.
authors: Trajectories of Recovery after ACutE and cRitical illness (TRACER) study group
articles.abstract: To examine physical activity levels in survivors of critical illness across 6 months, and to understand the barriers and facilitators of physical activity. Prospective, longitudinal, convergent mixed-methods study. Functional testing laboratory. Adults admitted to the ICU for at least 72 hours with acute respiratory failure or sepsis. None. Patients wore an accelerometer starting at hospital discharge, at 3- and 6-month follow-up to quantify daily step counts. At 6 months, physical function and patient-reported outcomes were collected in-person, with a subset of participants completing semi-structured interviews. Eighty-two patients were enrolled, with 67 (82%) having physical activity data with median age of 60 years (interquartile range [IQR], 52-66 yr), 54% male, and ICU stay 9.0 days [IQR, 5.8-17.0 d]. The median daily steps were 1358 (IQR, 742-2799) in 50 patients at baseline, 2305 (IQR, 1081-3898) in 54 patients at 3 months, and 2826 (IQR, 1609-4781) in 44 patients at 6 months. Higher comorbidity burden and earlier measurement associated with lower step counts. At 6 months, patients walked a mean of 344 ± 169 meters on the 6-minute walk test and reported being sedentary a median of 300 min/days (150-480 min/d). Eleven participants completed interviews, yielding three themes: 1) "a marathon, not a sprint": the extended ICU recovery trajectory; 2) engagement in physical activity is highly regulated by personal context; 3) value-driven and motivation-informed physical activity decisions. Mixed-methods integration demonstrated that qualitative themes expanded upon quantitative findings to explain nonlinear recovery patterns, contextualizing persistent sedentary behavior, and revealing that motivational and behavioral gaps are not captured by accelerometry. Survivors showed gradual improvement in daily steps over 6 months yet remained below recommended activity levels. Survivorship and attrition biases may lead to overestimation of step counts, further warranting larger studies. Integrating quantitative and qualitative data reveals modifiable contextual factors that may inform the design of pragmatic physical activity interventions.

articles.title: Evaluation of Sequential Organ Failure Assessment-2 Performance Across Demographic Subgroups: An External Validation Using MIMIC-IV.
articles.abstract: To evaluate the discrimination and calibration of the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA)-2 score for ICU mortality across demographic subgroups defined by age, sex, race and ethnicity, primary language, and insurance status. Retrospective cohort study. Single academic medical center in the northeastern United States (Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, MA), using the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care-IV database (version 3.1), 2008-2022, a dataset external to the SOFA-2 development cohort. Adult patients (≥ 18 yr) with at least one ICU admission. The first ICU admission of the first qualifying hospitalization per patient was analyzed. None. First-day SOFA-2 scores were calculated from the worst values recorded during the first 24 hours of ICU admission across six organ systems, with ICU mortality as the primary outcome. Discrimination was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and calibration using intercept and slope, with subgroup differences in AUROC estimated by bootstrap resampling. Among 64,015 ICU patients (mean [sd] age, 64.6 [17.1] yr; 56.1% male; 66.1% White), overall AUROC was 0.77 (95% CI, 0.76-0.77). Discrimination declined significantly with age: AUROC, 0.85 (0.83-0.87) for ages 18-44 years vs. 0.72 (0.70-0.73) for ages 75 or older (ΔAUROC, -0.14 [95% CI, -0.16 to -0.11]), with systematic underprediction in older patients. Discrimination was significantly decreased among non-English speakers (ΔAUROC, -0.04) but did not differ across documented racial/ethnic groups. Patients with missing demographic information had markedly higher mortality than the overall cohort rate of 7.2% (14.1% for missing race/ethnicity; 23.1% for missing language). SOFA-2 demonstrated good overall performance but with clinically meaningful variation across subgroups, particularly with age and language. Patients with missing demographic data experienced markedly higher mortality. These findings argue for routine equity evaluation as a complement to traditional validation of clinical prediction tools.

articles.title: The Effect of Guanfacine on Delirium in Surgical and Trauma ICU Patients: A Pilot Randomized Clinical Trial.
articles.abstract: To evaluate the feasibility of conducting a randomized controlled trial investigating guanfacine for ICU delirium, including assessment of recruitment, retention, protocol adherence, and data completeness, while estimating treatment effects to inform future trial design. Single-center, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial conducted from November 2020 to February 2023. Surgical and Trauma ICUs at the University of Alabama at Birmingham Hospital. One hundred critically ill adults with Confusion Assessment Method-ICU-confirmed delirium randomized 1:1 to guanfacine or placebo. Patients received 2 mg guanfacine or matching placebo nightly for up to 14 days, or until ICU discharge or delirium resolution. Primary feasibility outcomes included protocol adherence (target ≥ 90%), retention (target ≥ 80%), recruitment rate (target ≥ 2 patients/mo), and data completeness (target ≥ 95%). Most feasibility targets were achieved: protocol adherence was 100%, retention was 100%, and data completeness was 100%. Recruitment was significantly impacted by COVID-19 pandemic disruptions, achieving 0.9 patients/wk during active recruitment periods.For clinical outcomes, in unadjusted analyses, median delirium and coma-free days were higher with guanfacine than placebo (2 [interquartile range [IQR], 0-6] vs. 1 [IQR, 0-4]; p = 0.02); however, this association was not statistically significant after adjustment for prespecified baseline covariates. ICU and hospital length of stay and duration of mechanical ventilation did not differ significantly between groups. No hemodynamic differences or safety concerns were observed. This pilot study successfully supports feasibility for a definitive trial, with excellent protocol adherence, adequate retention, and preliminary signals that warrant further evaluation. Although adjusted analyses were not statistically significant, the observed unadjusted difference in delirium and coma-free days and favorable safety profile support progression to a multicenter trial informed by these pilot estimates.

articles.title: Composite Endpoints in Critical Care Delirium Trials.
articles.abstract: Delirium is an abnormal mental status, commonly occurring among critically ill patients, in which a person's attention and awareness change acutely. Delirium is associated with negative outcomes, including death. Furthermore, a longer duration of delirium is associated with long-term cognitive impairment in survivors of critical illness. Hence, there is a need for novel interventions that reduce the duration of delirium; however, measuring and analyzing "duration of delirium" as an endpoint in randomized trials is challenging due to the episodic nature of delirium and the competing events of coma and death, which can bias analyses of duration of delirium. Given these challenges, delirium trials have adopted one of two composite endpoints: delirium- and coma-free days, defined as the number of days alive without delirium or coma for both survivors and nonsurvivors, and an alternative composite that ranks death as the worst state and orders days alive without delirium or coma among survivors. To date, these composite endpoints have not been rigorously evaluated. Hence, herein we use data from the Maximizing Efficacy of Targeted Sedation and Reducing Neurologic Dysfunction (MENDS) trial to motivate the use of composite endpoints in critical care delirium trials, discuss how to define the effect of treatment on each composite endpoint and their clinical interpretability, and present a method for visualizing how the treatment effects accrue over the course of follow-up. Based on these analyses, we provide practical recommendations for the use of composite endpoints in critical care delirium trials, which could be extended to other randomized trials that rely on similar composite endpoints.

articles.title: From sirens to systems: Characterizing EMS and trauma care across America.
articles.journal: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery
articles.abstract: State emergency medical services (EMS) and trauma systems determine prehospital triage, transport, trauma center designation, data reporting, and quality improvement, yet their contemporary organization has not been systematically characterized. We sought to describe state-level EMS and trauma system structures, policies, resources, and perceived gaps across the United States. We conducted a cross-sectional survey of EMS and trauma system leaders in all 50 states and the District of Columbia from July 2025 through March 2026. A 56-item instrument utilizing categorical, Likert-type, rank-order, and free-text items assessed oversight, prehospital triage and transport, clinical protocols, trauma center verification, registries, quality improvement, and funding. Respondents were recruited by email and phone. Multiple respondents could contribute complementary domain-level information to a single state profile. Responses were summarized descriptively. All 51 jurisdictions participated. Most states reported a state EMS medical director (84%), statewide trauma triage protocols (84%), and mandatory participation in their state trauma registry (88%). However, operational coordination varied: only 29% had a centralized trauma communications center, only 6% of states reported a single point of contact for helicopter EMS dispatch, and 35% required a certificate of need for new helicopter services. Trauma center verification relied on American College of Surgeons (ACS) verification in 59% of states, while others used state-administered processes. More than half of states rated EMS financial resources in the two lowest adequacy categories, and 55% reported that their trauma system required at least moderate improvement. Rural populations were most frequently identified as underserved (96%) and as experiencing worse outcomes (92%). State EMS and trauma systems share broad adoption of national clinical standards but differ substantially in governance, coordination, verification, data integration, and funding. Level V, Prognostic/epidemiological.

articles.title: Normocapnia Versus Mild Hypercapnia During Lung Protective Ventilation in Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome: A Target Trial Emulation.
articles.abstract: This trial emulation aimed to answer the question: Among patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) who receive lung protective ventilation with low tidal volume, is normocapnia through an increase in respiratory rate associated with lower mortality than mild hypercapnia? Target trial emulation. Hospitals of the ARDS Network and Prevention and Early Treatment of Acute Lung Injury (PETAL) Network. Patients with ARDS enrolled in seven ARDS Network and PETAL Network randomized controlled trials. None. A target trial was emulated, assigning participants in a 1:1 ratio to normocapnia (target Paco2 35-45 mm Hg) or mild hypercapnia (target Paco2 50-55 mm Hg) for 4 days following the initiation of lung protective ventilation. The primary outcome was 90-day in-hospital mortality. Of 5367 potentially eligible subjects, 292 patients were assigned to normocapnia and 292 to mild hypercapnia. Separation in Paco2 values was preserved over the 4-day period of emulated intervention. Both groups had median pH greater than or equal to 7.33. Bicarbonate levels, driving pressure, tidal volume, and dead-space fraction did not differ clinically significantly between groups, while median respiratory rate was 33.0 breaths/min in the normocapnia vs. 28.0 breaths/min in the mild hypercapnia group (p < 0.001). Death within 90 days occurred in 84 of 292 patients (28.8%) in the normocapnia group and in 84 of 292 patients (28.8%) in the mild hypercapnia group (log-rank p = 0.842). This result persisted in subgroups such as older (≥ 65 yr) and obese (body mass index ≥ 30 kg/m2) patients. Among patients with ARDS who received lung protective ventilation, normocapnia through an increase in respiratory rate was not associated with lower mortality than mild hypercapnia. As this finding is derived from a trial emulation, it should be interpreted cautiously given the potential for significant residual bias.

articles.title: Circulating Cell-Free Mitochondrial DNA, Delirium, and Long-Term Cognitive Impairment in Critically Ill Adults With Sepsis: A Prospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: During sepsis, circulating cell-free mitochondrial DNA (ccf-mtDNA) is released and elevated due to cell injury, augments the immune response, and may contribute to organ dysfunction. Delirium is common and deleterious during sepsis, but little is known about the relationship between mitochondrial injury and delirium during sepsis. We sought therefore to examine associations between ccf-mtDNA and delirium and other clinical outcomes during sepsis. Multicenter, prospective cohort study. Medical and surgical ICUs in university and community hospitals in Nashville, TN. Four hundred eighty patients with sepsis plus shock and/or acute respiratory failure. None. We measured ccf-mtDNA in plasma collected on multiple days (study days 1, 3, and 5) during sepsis and assessed participants bid for delirium and coma using the validated Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU and Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale. We then assessed survivors' cognitive function 3 and 12 months after hospital discharge using the Repeatable Battery for the Assessment of Neuropsychological Status. During sepsis, the adjusted odds of delirium were 7% lower for individuals at the 75th percentile of ccf-mtDNA compared with those at the 25th percentile (odds ratio [OR], 0.93; 95% CI, 0.86-0.99; p = 0.048). ccf-mtDNA was marginally associated with in-hospital mortality (hazard ratio, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.99-1.20; p = 0.08), but was not associated with coma (OR, 0.98; 95% CI, 0.90-1.05; p = 0.31) or 3-month (beta, 0.23; 95% CI, -1.58 to 2.05; p = 0.80) and 12-month (beta, -0.36; 95% CI, -2.13 to 1.42; p = 0.69) cognitive outcomes. In this multicenter, prospective cohort study, higher levels of ccf-mtDNA were associated with lower odds of delirium, a result that contradicted our hypothesis. This provocative finding should be interpreted cautiously until replicated and explained by future studies.

articles.title: Alarm Fatigue Across Critical Care Domains: Comparative Insights and Independent Predictors From a Cross-Sectional Multicenter Survey Study.
articles.abstract: Alarm fatigue, the desensitization to excessive false alarms, threatens patient safety and staff performance across critical care domains. It is unclear whether alarm fatigue differs between hospital departments. This study compared alarm fatigue among staff in the ICU, cardiac telemetry ward (CTW), and operating room (OR), and, secondarily, identified its independent determinants. Cross-sectional, multicenter survey study. ICUs, a CTW, and ORs. A total of 514 healthcare professionals working in the ICU, CTW, and OR. None. Alarm fatigue was assessed using the Dutch-translated Charité Alarm Fatigue Questionnaire, which includes alarm stress and alarm coping subscales. Participants also rated their self-perceived alarm fatigue on a 1-10 scale and the percentage of perceived false alarms. Telemetry staff reported the highest self-perceived alarm fatigue (B = 0.65; 95% CI, 0.06-1.24; p = 0.032) and perceived false alarms (B = 0.77; 95% CI, 0.23-1.30; p = 0.005), while OR staff reported the lowest (B = -1.01; 95% CI, -1.59 to -0.43; p < 0.001). Second, physicians (B = -0.13; 95% CI, -0.25 to -0.01; p < 0.031) and less experienced staff (< 3 mo; B = -0.34; 95% CI, -0.68 to -0.01; p = 0.046) reported lower alarm fatigue. Alarm fatigue varied significantly across departments and professions, being highest in telemetry staff and lowest among physicians and less experienced personnel. Targeted department-specific interventions and longitudinal research are necessary to mitigate alarm fatigue and enhance patient safety.

Efficacy and safety of oliceridine versus remifentanil for analgesia in mechanically ventilated critically ill adults (CO-ROAM): a multicenter, assessor-blinded, non-inferiority randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract: Remifentanil provides effective analgesia during invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV), but its utility is limited by opioid-related adverse events. Oliceridine, a G protein-biased μ-opioid receptor agonist, may decouple analgesia from these effects, but lacks evidence in critically ill patients. This multicentre, assessor- and patient-blinded, non-inferiority randomised controlled trial was conducted across 19 intensive care units (ICUs) in China. Adults receiving IMV were randomised 1:1 to oliceridine or remifentanil, titrated to a Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool score below 3. The primary endpoint was time in target analgesic range (TTR; non-inferiority margin -10%). Of 307 randomised patients, 304 comprised the modified intention-to-treat population (151 oliceridine, 153 remifentanil). Median TTR was 96.0% versus 92.3% (absolute difference 3.7%, 95% CI -0.3-5.7%). Oliceridine was associated with fewer mild-to-moderate adverse drug reactions (ADRs), occurring at 15.9 versus 22.2 events per 100 patient-days (IRR 0.72, 95% CI 0.52-1.00, P = 0.049), and a lower rate of respiratory depression during the study period (0% vs. 4.6%, P = 0.015). Post-extubation respiratory depression (0% vs. 7.9%, P = 0.005) and analgesic-sedation costs were both lower with oliceridine. IMV duration, ICU stay, and 28-day mortality did not differ. Subgroup analyses identified a nominal ADR benefit in patients with Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II > 17 and a larger nominal TTR difference in those without acute respiratory distress syndrome. Oliceridine provides non-inferior analgesia to remifentanil with a more favourable respiratory safety profile and lower costs in critically ill adults. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06454292 (registered June 11, 2024).

articles.title: Violent Reinjury Trajectories Across Injury Mechanisms: A Multicenter Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: Survivors of violent injury often experience reinjury. We sought to identify demographic and clinical factors associated with violent reinjury across different injury types. We conducted an observational cohort study of individuals with violent injury (ie, blunt assaults, stabbings, and firearm injuries) across 2 adult and 2 pediatric Level I trauma centers from 2016 to 2023. Covariates included age, sex, race, hospital type, insurance status, and social vulnerability. Our primary outcome was time to reinjury. We used multivariable Cox proportional hazards models to measure associations between each covariate and time to reinjury across injury types. There were 29,038 individuals with nonfatal violent injuries. Male sex (n=19,273; 66.4%), Black and other race (n=21,403; 73.7%), presentation to adult hospitals (n=24,200; 83.3%), public insurance (n=13,879; 47.8%), and living in an area with high social vulnerability (n=21,044; 72.5%) were associated with a greater risk of any violent reinjury, adjusting for covariates. For index firearm injuries, patients younger than18 years had greater risk of firearm reinjury than patients aged 18 to 26 years (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR]:0.65 [0.47 to 0.91]) and for those older than 26 years (aHR:0.47 [0.34 to 0.66]). Although women with firearm injury had a lower risk of firearm reinjury compared with men (aHR:0.46 [0.36 to 0.58]), they had greater risk of blunt reinjury (aHR:1.77 [1.34 to 1.24]). Patients living in areas with high social vulnerability had a higher risk of escalating reinjury mechanism (eg, blunt to firearm; aHR:1.46 [1.11 to 1.90]) versus patients in areas with low/average social vulnerability. This research underscores how sequelae of violent reinjury are shaped by certain demographic and clinical characteristics, highlighting opportunities to strengthen reinjury prevention in key subgroups.

articles.title: Unintended Exposure to Medical Aid in Dying Drug Mixtures: Principles of Emergency Care.
articles.abstract: Medical Aid in Dying (MAID) is a legal medical option for terminally ill patients with decision-making capacity to self-administer prescription medication to cause death. MAID has expanded across the United States, with New York becoming the most recent state to legalize it in August 2026. As these medications become more available in the community, typically administered outside controlled medical settings, such as the home, rare but consequential unintended exposures can occur. MAID is distinct from euthanasia in that the patient must have decision-making capacity and must be able to self-administer the medication; this requirement contributes to the presence of highly lethal drug mixtures in nonclinical environments. Although MAID formulations are designed to be lethal, unintended recipients may ingest only a partial dose (eg, a "sip"), making survival possible with prompt medical care. We review the background and common components of MAID mixtures, which typically combine a sedative (benzodiazepine and/or barbiturate), an opioid, and cardiotoxic agents such as digoxin, β-blockers, and/or tricyclic antidepressants. We propose preliminary management guidelines for suspected unsanctioned MAID exposures: early regional poison center consultation; supportive resuscitation; activated charcoal when safe; targeted diagnostics, including serum digoxin concentration and serial electrocardiograms; gastric aspiration, when feasible; use of digoxin immune Fab when indicated; avoidance of flumazenil and naloxone in mixed ingestions; and substance-specific therapies, such as high-dose insulin for propranolol toxicity and sodium bicarbonate for tricyclic antidepressants-induced QRS widening.

articles.title: The Post-Sepsis Neutrophil: Lymphocyte Ratio: A Population Signal in Search of Individual Meaning.
Association Between the Neutrophil:Lymphocyte Ratio After Hospitalization for Sepsis and Long-Term Outcomes: A Population-Based Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: Long-term outcomes after sepsis survival remain poor. No clinical laboratory tests are in use for stratifying long-term risk after sepsis, limiting the development of secondary prevention. The peripheral blood neutrophil:lymphocyte ratio (NLR) reflects innate and adaptive immune cell balance, and may reflect an immune milieu which is associated with long-term risk after sepsis. Accordingly, we evaluated the association between the NLR in the weeks after sepsis hospitalization discharge-a time when patients are routinely seen in post-ICU clinics-and long-term outcomes. Population-based cohort study. Ontario, Canada, 2010-2020. Adults discharged alive from a sepsis hospitalization. None. The exposure was the first outpatient NLR-derived from the complete blood count-measured 15-90 days after sepsis discharge. Among 37,250 survivors with available NLR, the median (interquartile range [IQR]) time-to-measurement was 34 days (22-54 d), and the median NLR was 2.7 (1.8-4.2). Within 1 year, 17,732 patients (47.6%) were rehospitalized or died (median [IQR] time-to-event, 82 d [27-185 d]). The frequency of rehospitalization or death increased across increasing NLR quartiles: 34.2%, 41.5%, 50.3%, and 64.4% (ptrend < 0.001). Compared with the lowest quartile, adjusted hazard ratios (95% CI) were 1.24 (1.18-1.29), 1.54 (1.48-1.62), and 2.25 (2.15-2.35) across higher quartiles. For most patients, NLR after sepsis returned to its patient-specific presepsis ambient level, which was itself prognostic. Among sepsis survivors, outpatient NLR measured 15-90 days after discharge is strongly associated with 1-year risk of rehospitalization or death. As a simple, widely available biomarker, the NLR may support early postsepsis risk stratification and inform development of secondary prevention strategies.

Is a Minute Saved More Than a Minute Earned? Ambient Scribes and the Work Behind the Note.
Metabolic Failure and EEG Abnormalities After Cardiac Arrest: Which Comes First, the Chicken or the Egg?
Tenecteplase for isolated central retinal artery occlusion secondary to internal carotid artery dissection: A case report.
articles.journal: The American journal of emergency medicine
articles.abstract: Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) is a blinding neuro-ophthalmologic emergency. Internal carotid artery dissection (ICAD) is a rare but underrecognized etiology of CRAO, frequently missed at initial presentation due to absence of pathognomonic clinical signs. While early intravenous thrombolysis confers benefit in CRAO, evidence for tenecteplase (TNK) in ICAD-associated cases remains exceedingly sparse. A 44-year-old previously healthy woman presented with isolated acute left CRAO after routine jogging. Intravenous TNK (0.25 mg/kg) administered within 3 h of onset achieved complete visual recovery the next day. Cervicocephalic vascular imaging confirmed left ICAD. Six-month follow-up after dual antiplatelet therapy demonstrated favorable recanalization, stable visual function, and no cerebral or ocular ischemic events occurred. This case suggests that intravenous TNK thrombolysis within the therapeutic window can yield favorable visual outcomes and acceptable safety in patients with ICAD-associated CRAO. For patients with acute visual loss occurring after exercise, ICAD must be actively suspected. Prompt cervicocephalic vascular etiological assessment alongside emergency care, delivered via multidisciplinary stroke pathways for improved long-term prognosis.

articles.title: Trends in Care and Outcomes Among Emergency Department Patients With Chest Pain Without Myocardial Infarction.
articles.abstract: To characterize trends in hospitalization, downstream care, and outcomes among emergency department (ED) patients with chest pain without acute myocardial infarction (AMI) diagnosis. We analyzed claims data from a large national commercial insurer (2007-2021) and identified ED visits with a principal diagnosis of chest pain. We excluded visits with secondary diagnoses of AMI or other significant cardiopulmonary conditions and those preceded by cardiac testing, coronary procedures, AMI admissions, or chest pain ED visits within 6 months. Usage outcomes included index hospitalization (principal), 7-day cardiac testing, and 30-day coronary revascularization. The principal clinical outcome was 180-day postindex AMI hospitalization. Adjusted annual rates were estimated using generalized estimating equations, and trends were assessed using inverse-variance-weighted linear regression. We included 773,250 index chest pain ED visits (mean age 54.2 years; 54.3% women). Adjusted hospitalization rates declined from 42.7% to 18.6%, and 7-day noninvasive testing decreased from 26.7% to 9.1%. Revascularization within 30 days declined from 5.8% to 3.6%. Overall, 180-day postindex AMI hospitalization showed no significant temporal trend, ranging from 0.8% to 1.2%. However, a modest increasing trend was observed among patients aged 70 years and older. Among ED patients with chest pain without AMI diagnosis, hospitalization, cardiac testing, and revascularization declined substantially from 2007 to 2021. Overall, downstream AMI hospitalization remained stable, although those in older adults experienced modest rises. Although efforts continue to identify additional low-risk patients for safe discharge, future research should quantify the potential benefits of hospitalization and cardiac testing, particularly for older adults and high-risk patients.

articles.title: Concepts in Practice: Understanding and Addressing Name-Based Microaggressions in Health Care.
articles.abstract: Names are important markers of identity, culture, and belonging. In health care settings, individuals with ethnically distinct names may experience repeated mispronunciations, unsolicited nicknames, or avoidance of their names. Repeated mispronunciations without sincere efforts to learn or improve, as well as the avoidance, dismissal, or replacement of names with unsolicited nicknames, may function as name-based microaggressions and can negatively affect psychological safety, professional identity formation, and workplace inclusion. In this manuscript, we discuss the effect of name-based microaggressions on health care professionals and trainees, with particular focus on the emergency department. We review the 3 major categories of microaggressions-microassaults, microinsults, and microinvalidations-and use clinical vignettes to demonstrate how these behaviors may appear in both interpersonal and institutional settings. We also propose practical interpersonal and institutional strategies to promote more inclusive workplaces and foster respectful engagement with ethnically distinct names. By encouraging greater awareness, curiosity, humility, and intentionality around names, health care organizations can help cultivate clinical environments where individuals feel respected, included, and valued.

articles.title: A High-Yield Solution to the Emergency Medicine Resident Scholarly Activity Requirement.
Live Versus Delayed Video-Based TEAM Assessment During Real-World Cardiac Arrest: Agreement and Exploratory Differences by Rater Experience.
articles.abstract: To evaluate agreement between immediate live and delayed video-based assessment of nontechnical skills during real-world adult cardiac arrest resuscitation, and whether agreement differed by rater experience. We conducted a prospective observational study of adult cardiac arrest resuscitations in a tertiary emergency department in Taiwan in 2024. For each event, one trained physician or nurse who participated in the resuscitation completed the Team Emergency Assessment Measure (TEAM) immediately afterward and re-rated the same event from video approximately 30 days later. Live-video agreement was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients and Bland-Altman analysis. Of 105 recorded resuscitations, 80 had complete paired assessments. Mean global ratings were similar between modalities (8.25 versus 8.22; mean paired difference, -0.03; 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.25 to 0.20), whereas teamwork scores were modestly lower on video review (mean paired difference, -1.00; 95% CI -1.77 to -0.23). Event-level agreement was limited: intraclass correlation coefficients were 0.21 (95% CI 0.00 to 0.41) for total TEAM score and 0.16 (95% CI -0.06 to 0.37) for global rating. Total TEAM video ratings averaged 1.24 points lower than live ratings, with limits of agreement from -12.28 to 9.80. Agreement was higher among senior raters. Delayed video-based TEAM assessment produced similar group-level scores but limited event-level agreement during real-world cardiac arrest. Agreement appeared higher among senior raters. Video review may support debriefing and monitoring, but appraisal of a specific resuscitation or other higher stakes use likely requires experienced raters and structured safeguards.

articles.title: Controlling time-related biases in ECPR observational studies.
Efficacy and Safety of Ulinastatin in the Treatment of Patients with Sepsis: The ADJUST Trial.
articles.abstract: Urinary trypsin inhibitor (ulinastatin, UTI) has shown potential survival benefits in sepsis; however, conclusive clinical evidence is lacking. In patients with sepsis, does adjunctive ulinastatin, compared with placebo, reduce 28-day all-cause mortality? In this multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, adult ICU patients with sepsis meeting Sepsis-3 criteria within 48 hours of admission were randomized (1:1) to receive intravenous UTI (400,000 IU every 8 hours) or placebo, for up to 10 days in addition to standard care. Randomization was stratified by site and septic shock. The primary endpoint was 28-day all-cause mortality. Secondary endpoints included ICU, hospital, and 90-day mortality, and ICU/hospital length of stay. Of 347 patients randomized, 340 (169 UTI, 171 placebo) received intervention and were included in the safety analysis; after 5 post-intervention withdrawals, 335 (165 UTI, 170 placebo) were included in the intention-to-treat analysis. At 28 days, death had occurred in 39 of 165 patients (23.6%) in the UTI group and in 39 of 170 patients (22.9%) in the placebo group (absolute difference, 0.7% [95% CI -8.4% to 9.7%]; P = .98; hazard ratio 1.03, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.61, P = .90). Secondary outcomes were similar in the two groups. Adverse events occurred in 56.8% (96/169) of UTI and 42.7% (73/171) of placebo patients (absolute difference 14.1%, 95% CI 3.6%-24.6%; P = 0.009). In patients with sepsis, adjunctive UTI did not reduce mortality compared with placebo. Routine use of UTI for sepsis is not supported by these findings. ClinicalTrials.gov; https://clinicaltrials.gov; NCT02647554.

articles.title: Transfer of prehospital defibrillator recordings to receiving hospitals after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a 16-year retrospective study in Paris.
Calculating trauma undertriage rates: Are we using the wrong formula-and the wrong definition?
articles.journal: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery
articles.abstract: Undertriage (UT) is central to trauma center quality improvement, yet UT definitions vary, and no data-driven consensus target exists for interfacility benchmarking. We compared facility-level UT rates across four methods and assessed the impact on facility benchmarking. This retrospective study included patients aged 18 to 89 from Level I & II trauma centers in the ACS TQP Files (2021-2023). Facility-level UT was calculated using the Cribari Matrix Method (CMM), modified Cribari Matrix Method (mCMM), Standardized Triage Assessment Tool (STAT), and High-Intensity Time-Sensitive (HITS) intervention-based definition representing trauma team actions. Paired facility-level UT rates were compared across methods. To estimate benchmarking impact, we calculated within-facility rank change (higher rank = higher UT) relative to CMM. 2,643,881 patients and 515 facilities were included. Median facility-level UT significantly differed by method: CMM 11% [interquartile range: 9-14], mCMM 60% [50-67], STAT 6% [5-8], and HITS 30% [22-40] (all P<0.001). At individual hospitals, the median range of maximum UT values between methods was 53% [44-60]. The median absolute facility rank change between the CMM method and other tools was 129 [54.5-236.5] for mCMM, 48 [17-90] for STAT, and 142 [62.5-252.5] for HITS. These UT data highlight a concerning level of variation and uncertainty in the calculation and interpretation of a key trauma center performance metric. Until a UT definition is standardized and data-driven UT target goals established, cross-center benchmarking using UT should be interpreted cautiously and may be better suited for within-center trending. Level III, therapeutic/care management.

articles.title: Vasopressors as immunomodulators: a hidden axis in septic shock.
Pooled prevalence of infectious diseases among first responders in the prehospital setting: A systematic review with meta-analysis by occupation.
articles.abstract: First responders often work in unpredictable, uncontrolled environments, where exposure to infected patients and contaminated environments heighten the risk of communicable disease transmission. Their higher infection prevalence compared with the general population has driven the implementation of personal protective equipment, vaccination requirements, safety protocols, and infection prevention education. The aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to estimate the pooled prevalence of infections among first responders in the prehospital workers including paramedics, emergency medical technicians, patient transport staff, firefighters, police, and police officers. Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science and PUBMED/Medline were systematically searched. Pooled prevalence estimates were calculated using random-effects models with restricted maximum likelihood estimation, with Freeman-Tukey double-arcsine transformation and back-transformation to the original prevalence scale. Heterogeneity was assessed using I², τ², and 95% prediction intervals. Meta-regression was used to examine potential sources of between-study heterogeneity, and small-study effects and potential publication bias were assessed using funnel plots and Egger's regression test. Risk of bias was investigated using the AXIS tool. Following the initial search, 34,874 articles were identified, of which 88 were full-text screened. Of these, 22 studies representing 19,188 first responders were included in this systematic review. The pooled prevalences of hepatitis B and C were 6.2% (95% CI 4.5%-8.2%) and 1.8% (95% CI 0.9%-2.9%), respectively. Around 4% (95% CI 2.6%- 5.9%) of the first responders had MRSA colonisation. Current or past infection with COVID-19 among non-vaccinated first responders was 13.6% (95% CI 4.8%- 25.9%), which reduced to 7.3% (95% CI 3.6%- 12%) after exclusion of studies with high risk of bias. Of the known study characteristics, geographic region significantly contributed to heterogeneity, explaining 36.7% of between-study variance, p = 0.039. Infectious disease prevalence varied across pathogens, occupations, and geographical settings among first responders. These findings should be interpreted in light of substantial heterogeneity and limitations in the available evidence but may help inform infection prevention, occupational health policy, vaccination strategies, and future research in first responder services.

articles.title: Direct ICU admission versus floor-to-ICU upgrade in geriatric patients with multiple rib fractures and flail chest: A national analysis.
articles.journal: The American journal of emergency medicine
articles.abstract: It remains unclear whether direct ICU admission benefits geriatric patients compared with delayed floor-to-ICU upgrade. The study evaluated the association of direct ICU admission versus floor-to-ICU upgrade with clinical outcomes in geriatric trauma patients with flail chest and thoracic injury, stratified by oxygenation compromise, frailty, and rib fracture burden. This retrospective cohort study used the 2017-2024 ACS-TQIP-PUF to identify patients aged 65 years or older with blunt trauma, flail chest, at least three rib fractures, an Injury Severity Score of 9 or greater, and thoracic injury. Patients were classified as floor admission without ICU upgrade, direct ICU admission, or floor-to-ICU upgrade. The primary adjusted analysis compared direct ICU admission with floor-to-ICU upgrade, using floor-to-ICU upgrade as the reference group. A total of 6743 patients were included. Mortality did not differ significantly between direct ICU admission and floor-to-ICU upgrade in the primary adjusted analysis (aOR 0.732, 95% CI 0.467-1.148, p = 0.174). Direct ICU admission was associated with lower odds of unplanned intubation (aOR 0.355, 95% CI 0.251-0.502, p < 0.001), ARDS (aOR 0.412, 95% CI 0.172-0.987, p = 0.047), sepsis (aOR 0.352, 95% CI 0.171-0.725, p = 0.005), and DVT (aOR 0.444, 95% CI 0.209-0.942, p = 0.034). Mortality was lower with direct ICU admission among patients with 3-5 documented rib fractures (aOR 0.535, 95% CI 0.296-0.969, p = 0.039), and the association with fewer unplanned intubations persisted across all subgroups. In the secondary analysis, both direct ICU admission and floor-to-ICU upgrade were associated with higher mortality, lower odds of discharge home, and fewer ventilator-free days than floor admission without ICU upgrade. Direct ICU admission was associated with lower odds of unplanned intubation, ARDS, sepsis, and DVT compared with floor-to-ICU upgrade. These findings support identifying at-risk geriatric rib fracture patients for direct ICU admission before deterioration occurs.

articles.title: Integration of multimodal large language models into point-of-care ultrasound documentation: A pilot study.
articles.journal: The American journal of emergency medicine
articles.abstract: There are no studies evaluating the potential to deploy artificial intelligence in the interpretation of cardiac point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) documentation. Telexy Health developed an image interpretation and documentation system using multimodal model extensions with video capabilities (MLLM) and deployed it on the POCUS manager QpathE. This study evaluated the MLLM's agreement to experts in identifying cardiac POCUS views and interpreting normal and abnormal examinations. This was a retrospective pilot study using cardiac POCUS studies stored in QPathE. The MLLM was applied to POCUS examinations until 350 examinations were reached, 100 normal, and 250 with pathology. MLLM view identification and interpretation were recorded using Qualtrics, with expert image review serving as the gold standard. The MLLM was applied to 370 examinations, with 20 failures. View identification agreed with expert review in 151 examinations (43.1%). Cohen's kappa showed fair agreement for apical four-chamber views between expert and MLLM, with moderate agreement for parasternal long axis, parasternal short axis, subxiphoid, and inferior vena cava views. The MLLM agreed with expert interpretation 86 of 100 normal examinations; the agreement varied by pathology with pericardial effusion, ejection fraction, aortic outflow tract, chamber size, and inferior vena cava having an agreement of 8%, 4%, 70%, 0%, and 12% respectively. While agreement in image interpretation was poor, this vendor agnostic workflow demonstrated the ability to integrate an MLLM model into image interpretation. While it should not be incorporated into clinical practice in this state, future model improvement may enable automated POCUS interpretation and documentation.

articles.title: The Impact of Undernutrition on Post-Tuberculosis Lung-Function: A Prospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract: Undernutrition is the leading driver of tuberculosis worldwide, yet its effect on the lungs of people who complete treatment is not well defined. Among adults treated for drug-sensitive pulmonary tuberculosis, is undernutrition associated with worse post-treatment lung function, radiographic severity, exercise capacity and respiratory quality of life, and does systemic inflammation mediate that association? Adults (≥18 years) with drug-sensitive pulmonary tuberculosis were enrolled at treatment initiation in India. We measured associations of baseline body mass index (BMI), mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC), and premorbid BMI with spirometry, chest radiograph score, six-minute walk distance and St George's Respiratory Questionnaire score. Plasma IFN-γ, TNF-α and IL-6 were measured at baseline and month 2; counterfactual mediation analysis partitioned the effect of undernutrition on lung function into direct and inflammation-mediated components. Of 156 participants analyzed, 76 (48.7%) had a ventilatory defect; 52 (33.3%) had airflow obstruction and 31 (19.9%) had restrictive spirometry. Each 1 kg/m2 higher baseline BMI was associated with lower odds of any ventilatory defect (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 0.78; 95% CI, 0.67-0.90), and BMI below 16 kg/m2 carried five-fold higher odds than BMI ≥18.5 kg/m2 (aOR, 5.08; 95% CI, 1.76-16.02). MUAC and premorbid BMI showed similar associations. Lower BMI was associated with restrictive spirometry (aOR, 0.74 per kg/m2; 95% CI, 0.59-0.89) but not airflow obstruction (aOR, 0.91; 95% CI, 0.80-1.03). Undernourished participants had higher baseline IL-6, which mediated 32% (FEV1) and 49% (FVC) of the association with impaired lung function. Undernutrition before and at treatment initiation is a potentially modifiable determinant of post-treatment lung impairment, with systemic inflammation mediating part of the effect. Nutritional assessment belongs in routine tuberculosis care, and nutritional support should be tested to prevent lung-function impairment in tuberculosis survivors.

articles.title: The impact of removing prior authorization for guideline-concordant maintenance inhaled medications for COPD: a population-based cohort study.
articles.abstract: Most patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) do not receive maintenance inhaled therapies in concordance with evidence-based clinical guidelines. Long-acting muscarinic antagonists (LAMA), the recommended first-line therapy, is underused, while inhaled corticosteroids (ICS)/long-acting beta-agonists (LABA) are often used in discordance with clinical guidelines. In July 2020, British Columbia's (BC) universal drug plan removed prior authorization requirements for coverage for LAMA medications and restricted coverage for ICS/LABA. What is the impact of this policy change on guideline-concordant maintenance inhaled medication use? In a population-based cohort study using provincial administrative health data, we identified patients with COPD using a validated case definition and followed them from January 2019 (18 months pre-policy) to December 2022 (30 months post-policy). Using interrupted time series analysis, we evaluated the monthly proportion of patients filling a prescription for ICS/LABA and LAMA, mean canisters dispensed, proportion of days covered (PDC), rates of ICS/LABA discontinuation, LAMA (re)initiation, and initiating LAMA as first maintenance therapy. We report absolute differences between observed and counterfactual outcomes at study end. The cohort included 47,583 patients with COPD (mean 71.5 years, 46.5% female, 31.7 months mean follow-up). Thirty months post-policy change, ICS/LABA use decreased by -1.3% (95% CI -2.4, -0.3) and LAMA use increased by 0.8% (95% CI 0.1, 1.6). There was no significant change in the number of ICS/LABA canisters dispensed, PDC or proportion discontinuing ICS/LABA. Mean LAMA canisters dispensed increased by 9.8 per 1,000 patients (95% CI 1.0, 18.7) and PDC increased by 1.5% (95% CI 0.5, 2.4). (Re)initiation of LAMA or initiating LAMA as maintenance therapy increased by 0.2% (95% CI 0.02, 0.3) and 34.8% (95% CI 22.3, 48.6), respectively. Total combined drug costs did not change. Changes to drug coverage in BC were associated with improved guideline-concordant medication use.

articles.title: Pretransplant Pulmonary Hemodynamics, Explant Histology, and Primary Graft Dysfunction after Lung Transplantation for Silicosis.
articles.abstract: Silicosis associated with progressive massive fibrosis (PMF) is a major cause of end-stage lung disease among workers in the artificial stone industry. Patients with PMF are increasingly referred for lung transplant (LTx) evaluation and there is emerging evidence of pulmonary hypertension (PH) in patients with advanced PMF. Among patients with PMF referred for lung transplantation, what is the incidence of PH and what are accompanying histopathologic pulmonary vascular aberrations? Retrospective single-center cohort study of prospectively-enrolled participants, providing granular data on the invasive hemodynamic profile of patients with silicosis-associated PMF, histopathologic data on pulmonary vascular aberrations, and clinical data on post-transplant complications. Clinical and sociodemographic variables were collected. Explanted lungs from patients with silicosis-associated PMF underwent detailed pulmonary vascular histopathologic review and were descriptively compared with PAH explants. The incidence of primary graft dysfunction (PGD) was evaluated and descriptive analysis performed to provide associations of clinical features and PGD incidence. PH was present in over 95% of 21 patients with silicosis-associated PMF who underwent LTx, with a hemodynamic profile similar to patients transplanted for PAH. . Silicosis explants showed confluent silicotic nodules, extensive fibrosis and hyalinization, obscuration or obliteration of vascular structures, and perivascular fibrohistiocytic infiltrates with extrinsic narrowing. Classic PAH-type arteriolar muscular hypertrophy and plexiform arteriopathy were uncommon. In exploratory comparisons, patients who developed PGD had more frequent pretransplant right ventricular dysfunction (71% vs 21%; risk difference 0.50, 95% CI 0.06-0.75) and a lower median TAPSE/RVSP ratio (0.27 vs 0.39; Hedges' g -0.93, 95% CI -1.88 to 0.02) than in those without PGD. These findings suggest that PH in advanced silicosis with PMF is very common and represents a distinct pulmonary vascular phenotype characterized by extensive fibrotic vascular obliteration rather than the classic arteriopathy seen in PAH.

articles.journal: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery

articles.title: PIEZO1 activation alters membrane remodeling and aggregability of stored red blood cells.
articles.journal: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery
articles.abstract: Transfused red blood cells (RBCs) actively contribute to post-injury hemostasis due to surface phosphatidylserine (PS) exposure. We hypothesized that storage sensitizes erythrocytes to the PIEZO1-induced, calcium‑dependent, PS externalization through calcium and protein kinase C (PKC) dependent activation of the phospholipid scramblase TMEM16F. Five units of type O whole blood were obtained for analysis at days 21 and 42 of storage. RBC PS was quantified by annexin V staining on flow cytometry at increasing extracellular CaCl₂ concentrations (0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 5.0 mmol/L), with and without the PIEZO1 agonist Yoda1 (0.2 μM), PKC agonist Phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA; 6 μM) and antagonist chelerythrine chloride (CC; 10 μM), and the TMEM16 family inhibitor niclosamide (2 μM). RBC aggregometry was assessed by multiplate. Data were analyzed by analysis of variance and mixed-effects modeling. PS exposure increased in a Ca²⁺‑dependent manner in both day 21 and 42 RBCs (p<0.001). PIEZO1 stimulation enhanced this response to a greater extent in day 42 RBCs, with greater change in PS at 1 mmol/L (2.21% vs. -0.44%, p=0.021), 2 mmol/L (7.36% vs. 0.53%, p<0.001), and 5 mmol/L (12.09% vs. 6.40%, p<0.001) CaCl2. Compared with calcium alone, Yoda1 and PMA (+61.3%, p<0.001 for both) produced similar increases in PS externalization, whereas PKC inhibition (-45.6%, p=0.009) and TMEM16F inhibition (-4.6%, p=0.99) negated the PIEZO1 response. Yoda1 agonism preserved RBC aggregability after 42 days of storage (51.2±39.0 vs. 2.0±3.5 area under the curve, p<0.001). Storage sensitizes RBCs to PIEZO1-mediated, calcium-dependent, PS externalization through PKC- and TMEM16F-dependent signaling. Given its endogenous mechanosensitive properties, pharmacologic PIEZO1 activation highlights a potential mechanism by which mechanical stress encountered during trauma and transfusion through the injured microcirculation may promote erythrocyte phospholipid membrane remodeling and aggregability, contributing to the procoagulant activity of transfused RBCs.

articles.title: Long-Term Mortality in Sepsis Survivors: A Population-Based Study During 15 Years.
articles.abstract: To evaluate long-term mortality among sepsis survivors in Catalonia over a 15-year period and to identify factors associated with increased mortality within 2 years after hospital discharge. Retrospective population-based cohort study. Acute-care hospitals in Catalonia, Spain. Adult and pediatric patients hospitalized with sepsis between 2005 and 2019 identified using the International Classification of Diseases, 9th Revision, Clinical Modification and International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision, Clinical Modification codes for infection and acute organ dysfunction. Patients who died during hospitalization, were transferred to another facility, or represented readmission episodes were excluded. None. Data were obtained from the Catalan Minimum Basic Dataset of Acute-Care Hospitals, with longitudinal follow-up through the Central Registry of Insured Persons. Comorbidities were assessed using the Charlson comorbidity index. Logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards models were used to identify predictors of long-term mortality. Among 296,554 hospital admissions for sepsis, 237,075 patients (79.9%) survived to hospital discharge. Of these, 42% died (99,571) within 2 years. Long-term mortality increased significantly with age, ranging from 5.8% in patients younger than 15 years to 62% in those older than 84 years (p < 0.0001), and with comorbidity burden (21%, 38%, 51%, and 67% for Charlson index 0, 1-2, 3-4, and ≥ 5, respectively; p < 0.0001). Neoplasia (hazard ratio [HR], 2.011), liver cirrhosis (HR, 1.562), and dementia (HR, 1.304) were the comorbidities most strongly associated with mortality. Longer hospital stays were also associated with increased mortality. A progressive decline in long-term mortality was observed during 2017-2019. Long-term mortality among sepsis survivors remains high, with more than 40% dying within 2 years after hospital discharge. These findings support the need for structured post-sepsis care strategies focused on high-risk patients, improved continuity of care, and prevention of long-term sepsis-related complications.

articles.title: Persistent gaps in health-related quality of life measures for older adult trauma patients: A systematic review.
articles.journal: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery
articles.abstract: Older adults experience persistent functional and psychosocial consequences after trauma, but it remains unclear whether commonly used health-related quality of life (HRQoL) instruments adequately measure recovery in this population. This systematic review appraised psychometric evidence and risk of bias for HRQoL instruments used in United States trauma cohorts that included adults aged 65 years or older. MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL were searched from inception through January 28, 2026. Two reviewers independently screened studies and extracted data. Risk of bias was evaluated using an adapted Risk of Bias in Non-randomized Studies-of Interventions (ROBINS-I) assessment. Studies evaluating an HRQoL instrument as the target measure underwent Consensus-based Standards for the Selection of Health Measurement Instruments (COSMIN) Risk of Bias assessment for each reported measurement property. Results were rated as sufficient, insufficient, or indeterminate and synthesized by instrument. Of 17,195 records, 19 studies were included. Studies most often examined isolated orthopedic trauma (n=7, 36.8%), spinal cord injury (n=6, 31.6%), other injury populations (n=3, 15.8%), polytrauma or systemic injury (n=2, 10.5%), and burns (n=1, 5.3%). Frequently evaluated domains included physical functioning (n=16), emotional or mental health (n=13), overall life satisfaction (n=13), social functioning (n=11), and physical symptoms (n=10). Although all studies used at least one previously developed patient-reported measure, none explicitly adapted or comprehensively validated an eligible HRQoL instrument for older adult trauma patients. Ten studies evaluated a target HRQoL instrument, contributing 33 COSMIN measurement property assessments: 19 sufficient, 10 indeterminate, and 4 insufficient. Overall risk of bias was low in six studies, moderate in eight, serious in three, and unclear in two. Existing studies show that HRQoL instruments have been used in trauma cohorts including older adults, but they do not establish validity for older adult trauma patients specifically. Future studies should evaluate promising instruments in cohorts designed around older adults' recovery priorities and clinical characteristics after trauma. Systematic Review; Level III.

articles.title: Shortening the Family Satisfaction in the ICU (FS-ICU): Development and Validation of a 12-Item Family Satisfaction Survey for Adult ICUs.
articles.abstract: To develop and validate a shorter Family Satisfaction in the ICU (FS-ICU) questionnaire that reduces survey length while preserving content and psychometric performance for quality improvement and benchmarking. The FS-ICU survey assesses family perceptions of care, communication, and decision-making and has been translated into multiple languages with implementation across diverse health care systems internationally. In a province-wide electronic implementation in Ontario, more than 40% of initiated surveys were incomplete, suggesting that survey length may limit practicality for large-scale quality improvement and benchmarking. Multistage study using provincial FS-ICU survey data and an independent multicenter validation dataset for item reduction, psychometric evaluation, agreement testing, and external validation of a shortened questionnaire. A 12-member expert working group, convened for a Critical Care Services Ontario initiative, used provincial web-based data from adult ICUs across Ontario to develop a shorter version, FS-ICUshort. External validation was applied to FS-ICUshort using a separate multicenter Canadian revised FS-ICU dataset. A 12-member expert working group led by Dr. Daren K. Heyland, including administrative staff, ICU clinical staff, patient experience specialists, and quality improvement specialists from Ontario, used provincial FS-ICU rollout data. None. Using empirical criteria and expert ratings, the FS-ICU was reduced from 29 to 12 items: seven in the satisfaction-with-care domain (FS-Care) and five in the communication and decision-making domain (FS-DM). FS-ICUshort showed high internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.93 for FS-Care, 0.86 for FS-DM, and 0.94 for total). Confirmatory factor analysis supported a two-factor structure with better fit than a single-factor model. Scores from FS-ICUshort closely matched full FS-ICU, with mean differences less than or equal to 1.1 points on a 0-100 scale and intraclass correlations of 0.97-0.99. External validation replicated these results. The 12-item FS-ICUshort maintains the core content and psychometric quality of the original FS-ICU while significantly reducing length, supporting routine use in ICU family experience measurement and benchmarking.

articles.title: Consensus on a core outcome set for ventilation trials in critically ill patients with acute brain injury: results of an international Delphi consensus study.
articles.abstract: Clinical research evaluating mechanical ventilation liberation in patients with acute brain injury (ABI) shows substantial outcome heterogeneity, limiting evidence synthesis. We aimed to develop an internationally endorsed core outcome set (COS) and a hierarchical composite endpoint for ventilation trials in neurocritical care. Following COS-STAD/COS-STAP standards, we conducted a 4-round international Delphi study. Candidate outcomes were identified via a scoping review. A multidisciplinary panel from 31 countries scored outcomes using a 9-point GRADE scale. Inclusion required >70% rating as "critical" (score 7-9) and ≤15% as "not important" (1-3). Two consensus meetings were held to categorize outcomes, select representative measures, and ratify a hierarchical composite endpoint. 78 stakeholders participated in Round 1; 60 completed all rounds (23.1% attrition). Fifty-four outcomes achieved Delphi consensus. At Consensus Meeting 1, these were organized into 16 categories; the highest-scoring outcome per category was selected. Three outcomes were not ratified due to disease-specificity (NIH Stroke Scale) or lack of universal applicability (brain death, coma-free days). The final COS comprised 13 outcomes across 5 domains: respiratory function, survival, complications, functional status, and quality of life. A 3-level hierarchical composite endpoint was ratified at Consensus Meeting 2: (1) intensive care unit survival, (2) no reintubation within 72 hours, and (3) days alive without mechanical ventilation. This study establishes the first COS for ventilation weaning trials in ABI patients. Widespread adoption of these 13 outcomes and the hierarchical composite endpoint will standardize reporting, enable meaningful evidence synthesis, and facilitate clinical translation in neurocritical care. Core Outcome Measures in Effectiveness Trials (COMET) Initiative, registration number 2320.

Emergency Response and Patient Transport in Remote Indigenous Communities: A Scoping Review.
articles.abstract: Prehospital and inter-facility transport, such as air medical retrieval and pre-birth evacuation, often move Indigenous patients in rural and remote settings out of their communities, where care is already shaped by fragmented funding and structural inequities; no review has mapped these pathways globally. This scoping review mapped evidence on prehospital emergency response and patient transport for this population. A librarian-assisted PubMed, Embase, and Scopus search was conducted for English-language publications on March 9, 2026. Eligible studies included an explicit rural Indigenous population with a defined prehospital pathway. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts and assessed full texts, and a third reviewer resolved disagreements. Data were charted using a standardized form and synthesized descriptively. Across eight countries, 76 studies met the inclusion criteria, primarily from Australia (n = 29) and Canada (n = 23). Air transport and medical evacuation was the most frequently described pathway (71%), followed by ground transport (51%). Explicit description of paramedic or emergency medical services (24%) and dispatch/9-1-1 (12%) were depicted less frequently. Additionally, pathways were commonly described but rarely evaluated: only 12/76 (16%) publications used an evaluative design, and no pathway was evaluated in more than 7 of 76 publications (9%). The most reported barriers were infrastructure and communications (92%), cost and jurisdiction (87%), and distance to definitive care (83%). All percentages describe how often a topic was reported across the 76 included publications, and not its prevalence in practice. An explicit cultural-safety framework was applied in 9% of the publications, and community-led governance of the research in 7%. The published evidence disproportionately described transporting patients out of their communities. Community first response and tele-support were described more often than their standing in the literature suggests; however, they were rarely evaluated, and Indigenous-led governance of the research itself was reported in 7% of publications. Low reporting frequency does not establish that these models are uncommon in application and practice. Future priorities include community-partnered evaluation of community-based capacity and telehealth-supported care, alongside the development of patient and family cultural safety.

articles.title: [Emergency medicine requirements for the resuscitation room and the resuscitation room team].
articles.abstract: The resuscitation room is the central interface between prehospital emergency medical services (EMS) and in-hospital emergency care for critically ill and severely injured patients. From an EMS perspective, requirements are defined for activation, prenotification, team structure, handover, overload management and feedback. Written activation and allocation criteria are required that are applicable in the prehospital setting and agreed upon by hospitals, emergency dispatch centres and EMS providers. Prenotification must take place through a continuously available, reliable communication channel, be actively acknowledged and enable transparent feedback on capacity. Paramedics must be authorised to activate the resuscitation room independently of the presence of an emergency physician. On arrival, a qualified and operational team with clearly identifiable roles should be available. Handover should be structured and as interruption-free as possible. The exploratory online survey showed that trauma resuscitation care is predominantly guideline-based and more often includes a written minimum staffing requirement. In nontrauma resuscitation care, written activation criteria and binding team structures were less frequently available. Although handovers were mostly standardised, substantial deficits existed in overload and diversion protocols as well as in interprofessional feedback structures involving EMS. These findings indicate a need for coordinated procedures, transparent capacity management and binding quality-assurance measures.
